cse-2015-3-cs-51.approach: Find forbidden latencies from the reservation table, form the collision vector, and search the state diagram for the cycle with the smallest average latency.

steps.title: Forbidden latencies
steps.body: S1 used at 1, 5 → latency 4. S2 used at 2, 4 → latency 2. S3 once. Forbidden $=\{2,4\}$; collision vector $C_4C_3C_2C_1=1010$. Permissible latencies: 1, 3, ≥5.

steps.title: State diagram
steps.body:
From $1010$:
- latency 1: $0101\lor1010=1111$; from $1111$ only ≥5 → back to $1010$. Cycle $(1,5)$: average $3$.
- latency 3: $0001\lor1010=1011$; from $1011$ latency 3 again → $1011$. Cycle $(3)$: average $3$.
- latency ≥5: back to $1010$, average 5.

steps.title: MAL
steps.body: Smallest average over the simple cycles is $\min(3,3,5,\ldots)=3$. (Lower bound = max marks in a row = 2, but no cycle achieves it.)

pitfalls: Answering the lower bound 2 without checking the state diagram.
cse-2015-3-cs-51.verification: Latency 2 is forbidden, so a constant cycle of 2 is impossible; any cycle using latency 1 must then take ≥5, averaging ≥3.

cse-2015-3-cs-52.approach: Each policy breaks one Coffman condition: I breaks hold-and-wait; II, III and IV impose a total order on requests, which breaks circular wait.

steps.title: Policy I
steps.body: All-or-nothing acquisition at start: a process never holds some resources while waiting for others → no hold-and-wait.

steps.title: Policies II, III, IV
steps.body: Requests in strictly increasing (II, IV) or strictly decreasing (III) order of resource numbers: in a cycle of waits some process would have to request a lower-numbered (resp. higher) resource than one it holds, which is disallowed → no circular wait. Direction does not matter, only consistency.

optionAnalysis.reason: II and IV are equally valid orderings.
II is valid.
I and IV are valid.
All four prevent deadlock.

cse-2015-3-cs-52.verification: Each policy alone negates a necessary condition, so each alone suffices.

cse-2015-3-cs-53.approach: If $A\le_p B$ and $B\in P$ then $A\in P$; membership flows backwards along reductions, never forwards.

steps.body: $L_1\le_pL_2$, $L_3\le_pL_2$, $L_2\le_pL_4$, so also $L_1,L_3\le_pL_4$ by transitivity.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
- I. $L_4\in P\Rightarrow L_2\in P$. **True.**
- II. $L_1$ or $L_3\in P$ says nothing about the harder $L_2$. **False.**
- III. $L_1$ and $L_3$ are unrelated to each other. **False.**
- IV. $L_4\in P\Rightarrow L_2\in P\Rightarrow L_1,L_3\in P$. **True.**
